note: The dictionary schema for scripts/leak-check.ts, and deliberately nothing else. `categories` is empty and stays empty: this repository ships the mechanism, never the vocabulary. A curated list of one domain's words identifies that domain precisely — the list is the disclosure, whether or not a client is ever named — so both the terms and the exemptions that quote them live in an overlay that never lands here, merged at run time with `--terms <path>` or the colon-separated `LEAK_TERMS` environment variable. Because this file matches nothing, a run without an overlay finds nothing and still exits 0; pass `--require-overlay` wherever the checker runs as a gate, and it will refuse such a run instead.

schema.note: Free prose describing what this dictionary is for. Scanned like any other text: only the term strings the file itself declares are suppressed inside it, so a name typed into a reason is still reported.

categories.name: A short machine-readable label, printed beside every hit and used as part of an exemption's key. Categories with the same name in two dictionaries pool their terms; a term already defined keeps its first definition, and the run says so rather than absorbing the merge.
categories.why: Why this whole category is banned, printed nowhere but read by whoever maintains the list.

terms.term: The string to ban. A multi-word term tolerates any run of spaces, underscores or hyphens between its words, and at most one line break, so it is caught in prose, in a slug, in an identifier and across a wrap alike. Matching runs on a normalised copy: percent-escapes decoded, invisible formatting characters dropped, everything composed to NFC, case ignored.
terms.word_boundary: True matches the term only as a whole word, false matches it anywhere. Use true for anything short or ambiguous, because an unbounded four-letter term fires inside ordinary English and a check that cries wolf gets switched off. A bounded term still catches an English plural (`s`, `es`, `'s`) and still catches the word at a snake_case or CamelCase junction, so an identifier cannot hide it. It does not catch every inflection of every language; that residue is the price of not drowning the run in false positives.
terms.why: Why this term is banned and why it uses the boundary rule it does. Printed beside every hit, so it has to read as a reason a stranger can act on.

exemptions.path: A repository-relative path, in the repository being scanned. A private dictionary may name a public path; the reverse is what this split exists to prevent.
exemptions.category: The category whose term is exempted here. Required: without it an exemption written against one category silently absorbs the same spelling under another, including a category its author never saw.
exemptions.term: The term exempted in that file, under that category.
exemptions.line: The line the exemption was written for. It is part of the match, with a tolerance of three lines either side, so an exemption covers the occurrence it names rather than every future occurrence of that spelling in that file. Edits that shift a line within the tolerance still match and are reported by --audit as shifted; beyond it the exemption suppresses nothing and --audit fails. Zero is special: it names the file's path rather than its content, and never matches a hit in the text.
exemptions.why: Required and non-empty. An entry without a reason is rejected rather than honoured, the hit it was hiding comes back, and the run fails: an unexplained suppression is the exact shape a real leak would take.
